title: From the Saturn to Sega Sammy, in 27 moments
lede: The console’s life, the money behind it and the rivals around it. Filter by thread.

events.title: Bernie Stolar takes over Sega of America
events.text: The former Sony executive becomes president and cuts the U.S. company from more than 300 people to about 90.

events.title: Sega confirms a new console, code-named Katana
events.text: The Japanese design, with a Hitachi SH4 processor and an NEC-made PowerVR chip, beats a U.S. design built around a 3Dfx chip.

events.title: A ¥35.6 billion loss
events.text: Sega Enterprises reports a net loss of ¥35,635 million for fiscal 1998.

events.title: Launch in Japan
events.text: The Dreamcast goes on sale at ¥29,800. Supply is limited by a shortage of NEC chipsets.

events.title: Peter Moore joins from Reebok
events.text: He is hired to run marketing for the U.S. launch and builds the “It’s Thinking” campaign with the agency Foote, Cone & Belding.

events.title: A ¥42.9 billion loss
events.text: Net loss of ¥42,881 million for fiscal 1999. Consumer product sales fall to ¥84.7 billion.

events.title: Electronic Arts stays out
events.text: Talks between Stolar and EA’s Larry Probst end without a deal. EA never publishes a Dreamcast game.

events.title: Stolar is replaced
events.text: Sega of America names Toshiro Kezuka chief operating officer and says Stolar is gone effective August 11, five weeks before launch.

events.title: 9/9/99: launch in North America
events.text: $199, 18 games, more than 15,000 stores. Sega reports 225,132 consoles and $98.4 million in 24 hours.

events.title: Half a million in two weeks
events.text: Sega says 514,000 consoles have been sold in the United States.

events.title: Launch in Europe
events.text: Sega’s annual report dates the European launch to October 1999.

events.title: Okawa says it may be the last console
events.text: The Register later recalled that chairman Isao Okawa said in November 1999 that the Dreamcast would be Sega’s last console.

events.title: Peak year, and a third straight loss
events.text: 4.65 million consoles sold in the fiscal year, 5.55 million in all. Net loss ¥42,880 million.

events.title: PlayStation 2 launches in Japan
events.text: Sony’s console arrives in Japan first; the U.S. launch follows in October.

events.title: Moore becomes president of Sega of America
events.text: He holds the job until January 2003.

events.title: Sega moves against pirates
events.text: After the group Utopia shows that copied games can run from ordinary CDs, Sega says it has shut more than 60 websites and 125 auctions.

events.title: Price cut to $149
events.text: With a $150 rebate for buyers who take SegaNet for 18 months at $21.95 a month.

events.title: SegaNet goes live
events.text: Sega’s U.S. internet service and online gaming network opens.

events.title: The “Manifesto of the Future”
events.text: Moore and Charles Bellfield tell Sega’s executives and studio heads in Japan that the U.S. company cannot stay in hardware past Christmas.

events.title: PlayStation 2 launches in North America
events.text: At $299, with EA’s games and DVD playback.

events.title: The Nikkei breaks the story
events.text: The paper reports that production will end on March 31. Sega of America says it “remains committed to the Dreamcast format.”

events.title: Sega leaves the console business
events.text: The board decides to stop production. The U.S. price drops to $99 to clear about 2 million consoles, and Okawa’s donation of his assets is accepted.

events.title: Isao Okawa dies
events.text: The chairman and president dies aged 74.

events.title: The bill
events.text: Fiscal 2001 closes with a ¥52.4 billion inventory write-off and a net loss of ¥51.7 billion.

events.title: GameCube launches in Japan
events.text: Nintendo’s console arrives; Microsoft’s Xbox follows later in the year. Sega makes games for both.

events.title: First operating profit in three years
events.text: Operating income of ¥14.2 billion on sales of ¥206.3 billion. Sega sells 7.07 million games for other companies’ consoles.

events.title: Sega Sammy Holdings
events.text: Sega Corporation and Sammy Corporation combine under a holding company.

events.title: The 2K studio is sold
events.text: Take-Two buys Visual Concepts and Kush Games from Sega for about $24 million in cash, with the 2K brand.
